    "license": "http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/","articleSection": "Articles","name": "Gender, migration distance, and spousal preferences among migrant workers in China","headline": "Gender, migration distance, and spousal preferences among migrant workers in China","abstract": "China is experiencing a decline in marriage and birth rates. However, there is a notable absence of comprehensive research on migrant workers\u2019 marital behaviors, especially with a focus on gender differences. Using survey data collected in 2020, this study sheds light on the interplay among gender, migration distance, and spousal preferences. Key findings reveal that compared with male migrant workers, females in China tend to favor finding spouses in their destination cities. As the migration distance expands, female migrants\u2019 willingness to marry locals diminishes more than that of their male counterparts. Moreover, the study reveals that both male and female migrant workers who own homes in their destination cities find it easier to marry locals. However, the effect of homeownership does not significantly differ between genders, contrary to traditional expectations that men benefit more from property ownership in the marriage market. These results contribute to the broader understanding of marriage behaviors in the context of migration and urbanization in China, challenging established gender norms. Click on a formula to zoom.</span></span></span></div><div class="hlFld-Fulltext"><div id="abstractId1" class="hlFld-Abstract"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="abstract">ABSTRACT</h2><p class="last">China is experiencing a decline in marriage and birth rates. However, there is a notable absence of comprehensive research on migrant workers’ marital behaviors, especially with a focus on gender differences. Using survey data collected in 2020, this study sheds light on the interplay among gender, migration distance, and spousal preferences. Key findings reveal that compared with male migrant workers, females in China tend to favor finding spouses in their destination cities. As the migration distance expands, female migrants’ willingness to marry locals diminishes more than that of their male counterparts. Moreover, the study reveals that both male and female migrant workers who own homes in their destination cities find it easier to marry locals. However, the effect of homeownership does not significantly differ between genders, contrary to traditional expectations that men benefit more from property ownership in the marriage market. These results contribute to the broader understanding of marriage behaviors in the context of migration and urbanization in China, challenging established gender norms. Through this, it offers a fresh spatial dimension to gender studies, enriching the existing migration literature.</p></div><div id="embedded-pdf-target" class="with-border"></div><div class="pb-dropzone" data-pb-dropzone="contentNavigationDropZoneAbs"><div class="widget gql-content-navigation none  widget-none" id="2ffb43c7-15dc-4c79-9e29-8e4bed9b3d1e">

    </div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S001"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e140">Introduction</h2><p>In 2023, approximately 44.6% of migrant workers in China were under the age of 40 (National Bureau of Statistics of China <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1003" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>). Unlike the older generation of migrants, the new cohort frequently engages in multi-regional mobility as a standard aspect of their urban employment (Fan and Chen <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1006" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2013</a></span>). This heightened mobility, coupled with evolving social institutions and personal experiences, has led to significant shifts in their attitudes and practices toward marriage and relationships. Consequently, this group faces increased risks and complexities in their marital lives, making their situation a focal point for scholarly inquiry and policy consideration. Moreover, China is confronting the societal challenges of low marriage and birth rates. The marriage rate has continuously decreased from 9.9‰ in 2013 to 5.8‰ in 2020 (Yuwa Population Research <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0077" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). Meanwhile, the birth population declined from 17.86 million in 2016 to 9.56 million in 2022 (National Bureau of Statistics <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1003" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>).</p><p>Prior research reveals two critical gaps. Initially, despite emerging trends, there is a dearth of studies on the marital behaviors of migrant workers, especially through a gender lens. Earlier, rural women working outside without their spouses were perceived as risky, primarily relegated to domestic roles and confined to rural settings (Chuang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0024" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span>; Fan <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0036" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2004</a></span>). However, changing societal views in China now see migration as empowering for women, enhancing their life quality and autonomy, and reducing stigma (An, Broadbent, and Yuan <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0003" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2018</a></span>). Despite these gains, full societal acceptance and transformation are pending, with married female migrants facing workplace disparities and fewer protections than their single or male counterparts. Young, single migrant women, while seemingly more independent in pursuing relationships and marriage, often face pressures from traditional gender norms that restrict their autonomy and push them toward conventional roles (Connelly, Roberts, and Zheng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0026" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>; Fang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0039" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2012</a></span>). Additionally, existing research often overlooks how varied migration experiences affect marital behaviors, tending to assume uniform migration patterns and focusing on broad trends like economic stress and social integration challenges (Mu and Yeung <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0058" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Chen and Wang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0021" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2015</a></span>). These studies suggest migration leads to delayed marriages, increased instability, and altered marital expectations, but fail to delve into how specific migration trajectories impact these outcomes, highlighting the need for more nuanced, individual-centric research on the diverse effects of migration on marital behaviors.</p><p>This study seeks to fill these critical gaps by focusing on the marital preferences of unmarried migrant workers in China, with particular attention to the roles of gender and migration distance. Specifically, it examines how gender influences preferences for local spouses and how these preferences vary with increasing migration distance. The study also investigates the role of homeownership as a critical variable, exploring its impact on the perceived ease of marrying locally and challenging traditional assumptions about its gendered significance. By adopting a quantitative approach, this research aims to uncover the spatial and gendered dimensions of marital behaviors, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between migration and marriage in China.</p><p>This research has several unique contributions. First, it introduces a gendered perspective to the study of migrant workers’ marital preferences, addressing the differentiated pressures and opportunities that men and women face in the marriage market. Second, it incorporates migration distance as a key variable, providing insights into how spatial mobility influences marital decisions. Third, it highlights homeownership as both a material and symbolic factor in shaping spousal preferences, offering new perspectives on how economic resources intersect with gender in the context of marriage. Finally, the study situates these findings within the broader literature on migration and urbanization, emphasizing their implications for both academic research and policy-making. For instance, understanding the gendered dynamics of marital preferences can inform policies aimed at supporting migrants’ integration into urban communities, while insights into the role of homeownership can guide housing policies to better address the needs of migrant populations.</p><p class="last">In sum, this study examines the intersection of gender, migration distance, and marital preferences among China’s migrant workers, contributing to a deeper understanding of the social dimensions of migration. By bridging gaps in the literature and offering new empirical insights, it aims to enrich the broader discourse on gender, migration, and urbanization.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S002"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e183">Literature review</h2><p>Understanding why people get married is central to analyzing the marital behaviors of Chinese migrant workers in this study. Marriage decisions are influenced by a wide array of factors, including age, educational background, socioeconomic conditions, homeownership, gender, ethnic background, religion, children, and emotional considerations such as love and happiness (Eekelaar <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0034" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2007</a></span>; Hewitt and Baxter <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0044" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2012</a></span>; Horowitz, Graf, and Livingston <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0045" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>; Stutzer and Frey <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0067" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2006</a></span>). Among these, economic factors often dominate as primary motivators for marriage (Horowitz, Graf, and Livingston <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0045" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>). In heterosexual relationships, marriage frequently functions as an optimal economic partnership, where men and women form unions to consolidate resources and improve financial stability (Liu, Chang, and Su <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0054" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2017</a></span>). An Australian study provides further insight into the role of financial and educational factors in shaping marriage patterns, particularly in a gender-sensitive context. It finds that homeownership significantly increases the likelihood of marriage for both men and women. Additionally, men with higher socioeconomic status are more likely to transition into marriage, while highly educated women also exhibit a higher propensity to marry (Hewitt and Baxter <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0044" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2012</a></span>). These findings suggest that both financial stability and educational attainment play pivotal roles in marital decisions.</p><p>Beyond these factors, social networks also emerge as critical determinants of marital behaviors, particularly among migrant populations. The literature highlights that social networks influence marriage by providing opportunities for social interaction, creating pressures to conform to cultural or societal expectations, and facilitating introductions to potential partners (Haggerty et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0042" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>; Valenzuela, Halpern, and Katz <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0070" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>). Migrant workers, who often experience separation from traditional family structures, may rely more heavily on extended social networks, such as workplace connections or community groups, to navigate marital decisions. These networks can shape individual preferences, provide emotional and logistical support, and even reinforce norms and expectations surrounding marriage.</p><p>Adding to these dynamics, China’s persistent gender imbalance in birth ratios further influences marriage patterns among migrant populations. The gender imbalance arises primarily from a deep-rooted cultural preference for males, especially in certain regions where families often lean toward having sons (Jiang and Sánchez-Barricarte <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0046" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2012</a></span>). In particular, research indicates that the central regions witness a more accentuated gender skew, influenced by intertwined economic and cultural factors (Li, Jiang, and Feldman <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0052" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>). Due to the relative paucity of females, females command a heightened bargaining position in the marital sphere. Such dominance extends beyond mere numbers, allowing these women more excellent selectivity and setting elevated benchmarks for potential spouses (Ebenstein and Sharygin <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0033" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2009</a></span>; Tuljapurkar, Li, and Feldman <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0068" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1995</a></span>). For example, they are often inclined to wed men of a superior socioeconomic bracket, allowing them access to enhanced living standards and resources (Bulte, Heerink, and Zhang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0011" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>). Research also showed that females prefer to marry partners from an equal or, more often, superior socio-economic background (Gilmartin and Tan <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0041" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2013</a></span>). This dynamic naturally exerts considerable pressure on men, especially migrant workers transitioning from rural settings to urban landscapes. Such individuals often need help with the challenge of having comparable educational opportunities to their urban contemporaries (Du <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0032" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>). The following section delves into the role of gender in shaping marriage behaviors among migrant workers, exploring how economic pressures and social norms diverge for men and women in the context of migration.</p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S002-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e241">Gender and marriage behavior of migrant workers</h3><p>Considering the economy as a factor in migration while being gender sensitive helps reveal the multiple motives behind migration (Lutz <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0056" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>). Such a lens examines different genders’ perspectives on marriage and the underlying economic calculation. Different expectations for domestic roles in marriage, as part of social norms in Chinese society, diverge men’s and women’s views on marriage. Different genders, hence, seek different values in marriages. Particularly for the economic part of domestic affairs, men have traditionally been regarded as breadwinners, while women have sought bread providers. These expectations may shape migrants’ attitudes toward economic factors in marriage decisions.</p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S002-S2001-S3001"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e248">As a burden</h4><p>The financial implications surrounding marriage, especially in Chinese society, are profound. Traditional norms dictate substantial economic responsibilities upon the groom and his family. These responsibilities include providing a marital home, often known as the “marriage house,” and other amenities, setting the stage for significant economic pressures (Wei and Zhang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0072" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>). This economic responsibility is especially burdensome for male migrant workers. Due to their often-limited income from working in urban areas (Choi and Peng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0023" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016b</a></span>) and rising urban property prices, many male migrant workers find it challenging to meet the conventional expectation of owning a house before marriage (Yang, Wang, and Eklund <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1001" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>).</p><p>Another dimension of this pressure is the historically rooted “bride price” concept. This practice involves the groom's family offering money or gifts to the bride's family (Jiang and Sánchez-Barricarte <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0046" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2012</a></span>). Over the years, the bride price has escalated in many regions, further exacerbating the economic challenges men face (Sambe, Avanger, and Agba <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0064" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2013</a></span>). Research by Zhao, Chen, and Li (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0079" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>) has also shown that the social implications of not adhering to these marriage-related economic norms can be significant. Men who are unable to provide the expected material conditions may face stigmatization, lowering their overall attractiveness in the marriage market.</p><p class="last">Furthermore, the growing commercialization of weddings, influenced partly by global trends and the desire to symbolize status and success, means even the wedding ceremony itself can be a significant financial drain (Li <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0051" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). Collectively, these elements contribute to the pronounced economic stressors associated with marriage for men in China, particularly for those from less affluent backgrounds or those working in lower-paying sectors.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S002-S2001-S3002"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e277">As an economic strategy</h4><p>On the other hand, female migrants find marriage migration an attractive and attainable means to meet their settlement goal (Fan and Huang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>; Gaetano <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0040" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>). They can treat migration as an opportunity to meet future spouses in cities, where they can “marry up” to gain upward mobility (Mu and Yeung <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0058" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>). Abiding by a gendered economic approach toward migration (Lutz <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0056" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>), the following paragraphs discuss how marriage as an economic strategy has been carried out and how it has been used as a ladder to achieve social mobility during migration in China.</p><p>Marriage as an economic strategy is not a contemporary phenomenon but has been practised throughout the decades in the new China context. The power dynamics of who gets to leverage marriage as an economic strategy changes over time and reflect a rural and urban dichotomy and the rise of female power. In the late twentieth century, women's role in marriage migration was generally passive (Song and Luke <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0066" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>) as the results of marriage migration largely depend on men’s decisions (Fan and Huang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>). The fathers and the future husbands negotiate the decision; women have less voice in determining their marriages. Especially in rural areas, the idea of value exchange as the essence of marriage is vivid. Accordingly, helping sons get wives is considered recruiting daughters-in-law as laborers for the family (Fan and Huang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>).</p><p>Coming to the 1990s1990, women's social status has been improved, and migration restriction in the hukou system has been lifted (Shen <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0065" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1995</a></span>). More rural females migrated to urban areas. These rural female migrants became the major population that wielded marriage migration: the weights and the players of different sides of the scale shift. Women became the players; they get to decide what weights to put and what weights to gain. One appealing reason for rural female migrants to do so lies in the persistent institutional constraints embedded in the hukou system. While formal migration restrictions have been gradually relaxed, the hukou system continues to structure access to social welfare, family-related benefits, and local public services in ways that disproportionately disadvantage rural women. Marrying men with urban hukou entails improving the standard of living, housing, social networks, other types of resources (Gaetano <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0040" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>; Qian and Qian <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0061" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2017</a></span>), and achieving social mobility promotion in terms of earning urban hukou (Dribe, Eriksson, and Scalone <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0031" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>; Liang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1004" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span> cited in Wang and Hu <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1002" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>). Through their narratives, rural female migrants articulated new values associated with marriage migration. There appear to be two sets of criteria, “conditions” and “affection” (Gaetano <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0040" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>). While “affection” is self-explanatory, the criterion of “conditions” embodies a series of socioeconomic resource planning. Women will carefully consider their husbands’ hukou, property status, occupation, and family backgrounds, which embody social and financial status (<i>ibid</i>).</p><p>However, the scale is not always in favor of female migrants. There appear to be several trade-offs in conducting marriage migration. This observation generally happens between rural female migrants and local men’s marriages (Jin, Zhang, and Yang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0047" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span>). For women, the marriage migration may result in a high personal cost (Davin <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0029" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2007</a></span>). To obtain the urban hukou, they trade off some of men's merits, such as age, financial capability, and well-being (Fan and Huang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>; Wei and Cai <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0071" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>). For example, they will marry local men who might be older, poorer than other urban locals, or mentally or physically disabled (Fan and Huang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>). Educated rural women compromise with husbands who might have lower degrees than theirs (Qian and Qian <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0061" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2017</a></span>). Generally, the cases validate that marriage is an economic strategy for female migrants. Their main appeal in marriage is to remain in the city.</p><p class="last">This form of marriage migration has also shifted in recent years as hukou’s effect on migration has been diminishing (Liu and Wang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0055" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Zhu and Chen <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0080" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>). Migration from rural to urban areas is more accessible than before in China. The change in the hukou system is suspected to mediate females’ perception of marrying men with urban hukou as they can obtain urban hukou more easily themselves. However, more recent research is needed to validate the speculation.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S002-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e360">Female empowerment</h3><p>Migration can serve as a means of social advancement and provide opportunities for occupational and social mobility (Dribe, Eriksson, and Scalone <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0031" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>; Mu and Yeung <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0058" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>). This can be explained by the fact that migrants generally choose to go to bigger cities that can provide these opportunities. Funneling down to female migrants, it is found that they tend to marry men who have better socioeconomic status, and that the further away they are from home, the more likely they are to marry better (Dribe, Eriksson, and Scalone <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0031" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>). Using marriage as an economic strategy can be one explanatory factor for the correlation. In the meantime, this study also examines changes in female migrants’ perceptions as another explanation.</p><p>During migration, female migrants are encouraged to marry of their own free will. The empowerment comes from different aspects, and majorly focuses on gender equality (Connelly, Roberts, and Zheng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0027" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>; Gaetano <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0040" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>; Li and Wang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0053" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>). Living in bigger cities, being exposed to urban cultures, participating in public life, and enjoying more significant social and economic resources (Connelly, Roberts, and Zheng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0027" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>), female migrants change their perception of gender equality during their stay in destination cities as they are more urbanized (Chen <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0017" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>). They gradually cannot accept the traditional gender norms and practices in their cities of origin and try to escape these constraints (Gaetano <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0040" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>). In pursuing an urban lifestyle, female migrants demand better choices and greater autonomy in marriage (Li <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0050" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2017</a></span>). They see the autonomy of courtship and marriage as a form of feminism (Gaetano <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0040" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>), motivating them to stay in cities instead of returning to their hometowns and giving up the power of choosing marriage.</p><p>China is not the only country where female migrants experience a change in lifestyle after migration. The literature has proposed that changing lifestyle through migration is a form of empowerment. According to the normal life theory, migrants’ accustomed perception of normal life changes throughout migration, reshaping their ideas about what a normal life should be (Bygnes and Erdal <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0013" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2017</a></span>). For example, in Poland, it is expected that females take on more roles in domestic affairs and childcare. However, in Norway, gender equality is high, and both genders share domestic and childcare responsibilities equally. The differences in everyday life motivate migrants to stay in Norway to enjoy the social norms, while Polish practices are not favored. That is to say, because of migration, migrants see different kinds of living and are empowered to choose.</p><p>Another consequence of female empowerment reflects on the diverging attitudes toward returning home. Young single female migrants who are also better educated are more likely to remain permanently in destination cities than their male counterparts (Jin, Zhang, and Yang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0047" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span>; Liu and Wang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0055" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Zhu and Chen <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0080" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>). Male migrants, compared to female migrants, tend to return to the countryside because it is easier for them to reclaim social status and reintegrate into rural life (Choi and Peng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0023" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016b</a></span>; King and Lulle <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0048" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>).</p><p>Moreover, returning home has different meanings for male and female migrant workers. Men who return to their native towns often find their societal standing enhanced, their urban experiences positioning them as bearers of modern knowledge and, possibly, increased wealth (King and Lulle <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0048" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). For women, however, such a return might entail stepping back into a more orthodox setting. Their liberties could be limited here, particularly in communities where male offspring are still highly prized (King and Lulle <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0048" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). This traditional preference can shadow a woman's life decisions, compelling her to weigh the familiarity of rural existence against the allure of modern urban freedoms.</p><p>Overall, it is suggested that female migrants are empowered by migration. Through migration, their perceptions shift. They are exposed to more lifestyle paradigms and can choose which kinds of everyday life they want. The pulling effect of gender equality in host cities and the push factor in terms of lagged social norms work as a pair of forces that mediate female migrants’ settlement intention and make them see that pursuing marriage is a freedom of choice. Therefore, female migrants tend to marry men in destination cities in order not to return home.</p><p class="last">Drawing from the detailed examination of the socioeconomic aspects surrounding marriage practices in China, especially the distinctive experiences of women in navigating the urban-rural divide, this study formulates the first hypothesis:
</p><div class="quote"><p class="first last">H1: Female migrant workers are more inclined to seek spouses locally (migration destination cities).</p></div><p></p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S002-S2003"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e435">Marriage preference: distance as a factor</h3><p>In the intricate web of marriage customs and traditions, each society possesses unique nuances influenced by its historical, sociological, and cultural background. One existing finding based on the Swedish society, which suggests that female migrants will marry better if they are further away from home (Dribe, Eriksson, and Scalone <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0031" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>), seems to be impractical under the lens of Chinese social norms and values. It is already shown that Chinese marital traditions, deeply rooted in ancient customs and further molded by modern socio-political policies, present a distinct pattern in which gender plays a crucial role in marriage migration decisions. In response to the correlation between marriage and distance, less is understood about how it would translate to Chinese society. This review delves into gender-sensitive aspects of how distance might affect migrants’ intentions in settlement.</p><p>Historically, it is patrilinear traditions that have influenced China's matrimonial practices, where lineage, inheritance, and family continuity are passed down through the male line (Hu and Scott <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1005" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span>). A central aspect of this tradition is the post-marital residence pattern, predominantly characterized by women moving to their husband's family residence after marriage (Fan and Huang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>; Xiong <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0075" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>). The move requires them to detach from their hometown, childhood memories, close-knit community, and, most poignantly, their immediate families. This distance, both physical and emotional, can be a significant deterrent. The daunting task of integrating into a new family is amplified when faced with the challenges of adapting to a new region with potentially distinct dialects, customs, and traditions. Besides, rural parents generally do not favor outsiders, or people from different provinces (Choi and Peng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0023" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016b</a></span>). The girls’ parents cannot see their daughters regularly and could not help if their daughters were abused (<i>ibid</i>). Young migrant women also find that living closer to home is a self-protection strategy as their family can act as a protector (<i>ibid</i>). Thus, the cultural practice of uxorilocal residence not only influences the post-marital living arrangement but also may shape unmarried female migrants’ perspectives and apprehensions regarding marrying into distant areas.</p><p>Filial piety is a core value in Chinese culture, emphasizing the importance of caring for one’s parents. This cultural expectation plays a significant role in marriage migration, as moving far away from parents can make fulfilling this responsibility more challenging. Although both male and female offspring express a solid intention to take care of their parents, in reality, women are the de facto caretakers. In a study about the impact of rural-to-urban migration on family dynamics focusing on male migrants, multiple interviewees indicate that their sisters or wives are the ones taking care of their parents (Choi and Peng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0022" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016a</a></span>). For example, a construction worker in Shenzhen said that it was his elder sister who took care of their sick mother; another excerpt indicates that it was the second son’s wife who took care of the son’s mother (<i>ibid</i>). Factoring in that women are the practical caretakers, it is reasonable to speculate that women may show a stronger intention in marrying to an urban place that is closer to their rural origins.</p><p>Moreover, China's One-Child Policy, which reshaped familial responsibilities, may strengthen this marriage pattern of female migrants. As single-child families became prevalent, the sole child, regardless of gender, was tasked with the care of ageing parents (Alpermann and Zhan <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0002" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>). However, women experienced unique pressures in this regard. Women traditionally joined their husband's family upon marriage, often bearing responsibilities toward their elderly relatives. Yet, being an only child meant their own parents had no other caretakers, leading to heightened responsibilities for women, especially when marrying into distant locales (Cai and Feng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0015" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>). Thus, this duality of care became incredibly complex when geographical distance from natal families was introduced.</p><p class="last">Based on the analysis above, the second hypothesis of this study is:
</p><div class="quote"><p class="first last">H2: Compared to males, the willingness of female migrant workers to marry locals decreases more significantly as the migration distance increases.</p></div><p></p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S002-S2004"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e483">Data and methods</h3><p>The data for this study were collected in 2020, focusing specifically on migrant workers in China. The survey was conducted across 46 cities with a high concentration of migrant workers, including major international hubs such as Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen, as well as coastal cities like Dongguan, Jiaxing, and Nantong. A total of 23,381 responses were received. The survey employed a stratified sampling method to ensure representation across various regions and demographic groups. Questionnaires were distributed both online and through local labor offices to maximize accessibility and response rates.</p><p>The dependent variable utilized in this investigation is termed “<i>partner</i>,” derived from the survey question: “Where do you expect your future partner to be from?” Respondents were presented with three distinct options to select from (1) “Local,” signifying a preference for a partner from the local area, from the current city of residence; (2) “Hometown,” indicating a desire for a partner from their place of origin; and (3) “Elsewhere,” suggesting a preference for a partner from a location other than the local area. (4) “don’t know.” Those who selected “don’t know” were excluded from this study. We interpret those who choose “local” possess an inclination for a partner hailing from the same local area. In contrast, individuals who select “hometown” or “elsewhere” express a lack of preference for a local partner. Additionally, married respondents and those who had migrated locally within the same city were also excluded. Local migrants were excluded because they are considered local residents and lack the distinct spatial and cultural dynamics that typically influence partner preferences in inter-city or inter-provincial migrations, which are central to this study. The final sample size for analysis was 2633.</p><p class="last">Given that our dependent variables are dichotomous, we utilize the binary logistic model to adapt the standard random utility model to address our research question on long-term resident intention choice. The model is represented as:
<span class="NLM_disp-formula-image disp-formula rs_preserve"><img src="//:0" alt="" class="mml-formula" data-formula-source="{"type":"image","src":"/cms/asset/42c25ab8-cf95-45f0-875a-3e866977290d/rage_a_2606824_um0001.gif"}"></span><span class="NLM_disp-formula disp-formula rs_preserve"><img src="//:0" alt="" data-formula-source="{"type":"mathjax"}"><math><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>ij</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>ij</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mrow><mi>ij</mi></mrow></msub></math></span>The main dependent variables considered in this article include <i>gender</i> and <i>migration distance</i>. The gender variable is derived from the personal information provided by the respondents in the questionnaire. The variable “<i>migration distance</i>” is established by the response to the questionnaire query: “<i>Where is your household registration (Hukou) located</i>?” If the participant selects “Different province from the place of employment,” it will be categorized as inter-provincial migration. Opting for “Same province but different prefecture-level city from the place of employment” or “Same prefecture-level city but different county from the place of employment” will be classified as intra-provincial migration within this study. Other control variables encompass personal characteristics such as <i>education</i> and <i>age</i>, migration characteristics including <i>migration distance, migration duration, settlement intention, employment, social network</i> and <i>wage level,</i> and destination characteristics including <i>house price</i> and <i>economic development</i> (Ln (GDP per capita)) (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0001" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 1</button>). Migration duration refers to the length of time respondents have resided in their current location. Settlement intention indicates the respondents’ long-term intention to reside in the destination city, reflecting their desire to establish permanent roots and integrate into the local community.
</p><div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 1. </span> Descriptive statistics (<i>n</i> = 2633).</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="T0001-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="/action/downloadTable?id=T0001&doi=10.1080%2F10225706.2025.2606824&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="T0001" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Display Table</a></div></div><p></p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S003"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e865">Analysis</h2><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S003-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e867">Descriptive analysis</h3><p>Our initial focus is on providing descriptive evidence to test the hypotheses. In <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0002" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 2</button>, we examine the correlation between the gender of migrant workers and their geographical preferences for a potential life partner. Among the male respondents, 370 individuals expressed a preference for a partner from elsewhere. In contrast, a significantly higher number of 1461 male respondents indicated a preference for a partner from the local destination, accounting for 79.79%. On the other hand, among the female respondents, 111 expressed a desire for a partner from elsewhere. In contrast, a notable majority of 691 females showed a preference for a partner from the local destination, accounting for 86.16%. The data reveal that female migrants are more inclined to seek life partners from the local destination than their male counterparts. This result is consistent with our H1, which suggests that female migrant workers are more inclined to seek partners locally in their destination cities.
</p><div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 2. </span> Migrant gender and geographical preferences for partner (<i>n</i> = 2633).</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="T0002-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="/action/downloadTable?id=T0002&doi=10.1080%2F10225706.2025.2606824&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="T0002" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Display Table</a></div></div><p></p><p><button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0001" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig">Figure 1</button> provides insights into partner preferences based on two levels of migration distance: intra-provincial (within the same province) and inter-provincial (between different provinces). The analysis highlights how these migration distances influence partner preferences for both genders.
</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 1. </span></span> Gender, settlement intention and geographical preferences for partner (<i>n</i> = 2633).</p></div><a href="#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="F0001"><img id="d1e957" src="/cms/asset/162f78e8-9397-44c2-bb56-e584a35818bb/rage_a_2606824_f0001_ob.jpg" loading="lazy" height="291" width="500" alt="Figure 1. Gender, settlement intention and geographical preferences for partner (n = 2633)."></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="F0001" data-popup-event-type="fig">Display full size</button></div></div><p></p><p class="last">For males migrating within the same province (intra-provincial), 82.28% display a preference for local partners. As the migration distance increases to inter-provincial levels, the inclination for local partners remains notably high at 76.49%. Similarly, when considering females within the same province (intra-provincial), a significant majority of 90.12% exhibit a preference for local partners. This preference for local partners remains robust at 76.67% even as migration spans between provinces (inter-provincial). Those data indicate that regardless of gender, individuals tend to have a stronger preference for host cities’ partners when the migration distance is shorter, whether within the same province or between provinces. Furthermore, females consistently exhibit a more pronounced decrease in preference for local partners compared to males, a finding that supports our H2.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S003-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e961">Modeling</h3><p>Recognizing the multifaceted nature of migrant worker experiences, this research endeavor aims to incorporate a comprehensive array of relevant variables to ensure a thorough and accurate analysis. Consequently, this section will delve deeper into the interplay among these three factors by employing logit models that also consider other relevant variables with the potential to impact the relationships under scrutiny. The models utilize the respondents who expressed a desire for their future partner to come from “Elsewhere” as the reference category for comparison. Notably, all models exhibit high levels of statistical significance. <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0003" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 3</button> presents the logit coefficients, standard errors, and significance levels associated with each estimated variable.
</p><div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 3. </span> Binary logistic model of migrant workers’ spouse preference.</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="T0003-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="/action/downloadTable?id=T0003&doi=10.1080%2F10225706.2025.2606824&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="T0003" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Display Table</a></div></div><p></p><p>Our Model 1 did not introduce any interaction terms (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0003" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 3</button>). The coefficient for the <i>gender</i> variable is positive and statistically significant, indicating that, in comparison to male migrant workers, female migrant workers are more inclined toward having local partners in the future. This result aligns with our H1. This inclination of female migrant workers toward local partners can be attributed to the various dynamics discussed earlier, such as the enhanced bargaining power they command in the marital sphere and the societal pressures males face in the competitive marriage market.</p><p>Moreover, as urbanization continues at its rapid pace, the appeal of city life and the opportunities it presents, both in terms of economic growth and personal freedom, weigh heavily on these preferences (Chen and Liu <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0019" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span>). Women, having adapted to the urban environment, may find it challenging to give up the advantages of city life, particularly when returning to rural areas might involve surrendering certain liberties and opportunities (Chuang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0024" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016</a></span>). This reiterates the notion that women's decisions in the marriage market are influenced not just by economic factors but also by a desire for a broader spectrum of life opportunities and escaping the confines of traditional structures.</p><p>Regarding migration distance, the model's results indicate that compared to migration within the province, migrant workers who move outside the province are less inclined to choose a spouse at their destination. This inclination can possibly be attributed to several factors. Firstly, Chinese culture places a strong emphasis on family and community, creating deep connections with one's hometown. This makes local marriages more appealing, as they help maintain essential relationships, provide a robust support system, and foster a strong sense of belonging (Bossen <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0009" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2007</a></span>). Additionally, selecting a partner from a similar cultural background ensures a foundation of shared values, traditions, and language. This, in turn, makes communication and understanding easier within the relationship and helps avoid potential challenges arising from differences in cultural norms that might occur with partners from distant regions. Practical considerations also come into play (Bossen <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0009" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2007</a></span>). Marrying someone from the same local area is more feasible for migrant workers due to the complex logistics of managing two households over significant distances. Being geographically close allows for easy family visits, active participation in local activities, and the smooth fulfillment of familial responsibilities (Choi and Peng <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0022" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2016a</a></span>).</p><p>Briefly addressing the control variables, among the individual characteristics, both age and education are significantly related to their preferences for a spouse. Model 1 indicates that as migrants’ age increases, they tend to marry locals. This trend could be attributed to several factors: older migrants may have had more time to adapt to the local culture and social norms, as supported by Berry's (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT1007" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1997</a></span>) acculturation theory. Additionally, older individuals may place greater emphasis on career stability and social connections, as they are more likely to prioritize long-term goals over exploration and mobility (Elder, Johnson, and Crosnoe <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0035" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2003</a></span>). These factors can make local partners more appealing, as such relationships often offer a sense of stability and community integration. Regarding education, the coefficient for migrants with higher education is positive, suggesting they may be more inclined to marry locally (at their destination) compared to those with lower education, but this result is not statistically significant in Model 1. This indicates that while higher education may be associated with better adaptability to new cultures and environments (Chen and Wang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0021" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2015</a></span>; Mu and Yeung <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0058" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>), such adaptability does not necessarily translate into a statistically significant preference for local partners.</p><p>Additionally, aside from migration distance, Model 1 also considers the relationship between other migration characteristic factors and spouse preferences. In terms of duration, the result shows that the longer migrant workers stay in the local area, the more inclined they are to seek future partners locally. However, migration duration exceeding 5 years does not show significance. Secondly, the model's results indicate a significant correlation between the wage level of migrant workers and spouse preferences. As the wage level increases, the coefficient is negative, indicating that respondents earning over 5000 RMB are more inclined to seek a spouse in other regions rather than locally, compared to lower-income individuals. This could be because higher-income migrant workers may have greater mobility and broader social networks, enabling them to connect with potential partners in different areas. Additionally, they might prioritize compatibility and personal preferences over proximity, given their increased financial capacity to sustain long-distance relationships or relocate if necessary. This finding suggests that higher wages may reduce the perceived constraints of geographic location in spousal preferences. Moreover, Model 1 suggests that there is no significant relationship between occupation and spouse preferences. Furthermore, migrant workers’ intention to reside long-term is significantly associated with their spouse preferences. Migrant workers who express a desire for prolonged local residency are more inclined to prefer a spouse from the local area. The results of Model 1 indicate that the social networks of migrant workers are also related to spouse preferences. Respondents who consider local connections to be necessary within their social networks show a notably higher inclination toward desiring a local spouse. This tendency may arise from their close connections to the local community, making them more inclined to seek a marital partner who shares a similar community background (Asadullah and Wahhaj <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0006" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>). This choice enhances their sense of integration within the society, as their spouse shares comparable social and cultural contexts, making it easier to adapt and understand each other's lifestyles and values. Consequently, their spouse preference is significantly influenced by their prioritization of local social integration. Lastly, Model 1 indicates that the local economic and housing price levels are not significantly correlated with the spouse preferences of migrant workers.</p><p>In Model 2 (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0003" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 3</button>), we introduce the interaction terms “Gender #Migration Distance” to test H2. The coefficients of the interaction term were statistically significant, suggesting that the relationship between migrant’s gender and their spouse preference varies with distance (see <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0004" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 4</button>). However, the coefficient of an interaction term in a non-linear regression is not a suitable way to understand the interaction (Mize <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0057" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>). Thus, to further examine the relationship between these two variables and the spouse preference of migrant workers, <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0005" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 5</button> shows the predicted probability of spouse preference for migrants with migrants’ gender by distance when all other variables are held at observed values. It is evident that as the migration distance increases, there is no difference in spouse preferences among male migrants. However, a significant difference emerges for female migrants. Specifically, the predictive margins decrease from 0.89 to 0.79. This result further supports our H2 that, in comparison to males, the reduction in the willingness of female migrant workers to marry individuals from the local area is more pronounced as the migration distance increases.
</p><div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 4. </span> Predictive margins of Gender#Distance with 95% confidence intervals.</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="T0004-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="/action/downloadTable?id=T0004&doi=10.1080%2F10225706.2025.2606824&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="T0004" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Display Table</a></div></div>
<div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 5. </span> Gender and homeownership of migrant workers.</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="T0005-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="/action/downloadTable?id=T0005&doi=10.1080%2F10225706.2025.2606824&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="T0005" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Display Table</a></div></div><p></p><p class="last">This trend can be attributed to several intertwined factors. Historically, China's patrilinear traditions have dictated post-marital residence patterns, often requiring women to relocate to their husbands’ families. This separation from their hometowns, communities, and immediate families creates emotional and cultural challenges, making the prospect of marrying into distant locales daunting. Additionally, China's One-Child Policy has intensified responsibilities for women, who are expected to care for aging parents and in-laws. Marrying into distant areas accentuates this responsibility, as women are often required to manage the care of both sets of parents from afar. Therefore, combining cultural practices and familial obligations contributes to a greater decrease in female migrant workers’ willingness to marry locals as migration distance increases.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S004"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e1484">Homeownership and spousal preference</h2><p>In China's marriage market, homeownership is not only a symbol of wealth but also a foundation for marital stability. The literature suggests that male migrant workers experience considerable pressure to acquire a home due to their greater financial responsibilities in marriage (Wei and Zhang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0072" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>). On the other hand, female migrant workers often prioritize whether their potential spouse owns property, as it represents economic stability and security. <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0005" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 5</button> illustrates the distribution of homeownership among unmarried male and female migrant workers. The overall proportion of unmarried migrant workers who own homes is low. The homeownership rates among males (7.97%) and females (7.73%) are very similar, indicating minimal gender differences. In this section, we will examine the relationship between homeownership and marriage behaviors among migrant workers, with a particular focus on how homeownership shapes unmarried migrant workers’ subjective perceptions of the difficulty in marrying locals.</p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S004-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e1494">Modeling</h3><p>For respondents who chose to marry locals, the survey further asked about their perceived difficulty in finding a local spouse, offering options such as “easy to achieve” and “difficult to achieve.” Over 57.9% of the respondents indicated that finding a suitable local spouse was relatively easy. Regarding homeownership, the survey asked respondents about their current living arrangements in the area where they reside, offering several options: company-provided dormitories (including construction site sheds), private rentals, government-provided public rental housing, purchased affordable housing, purchased shared ownership housing, privately purchased commercial housing, and staying with relatives. For this study, respondents who indicated that they had purchased affordable housing, shared ownership housing, or privately purchased commercial housing were categorized as property owners in the local area. The data show that approximately 13.6% of respondents already own property in the local area.</p><p>Next, this study uses respondents’ subjective perceptions of the difficulty in marrying locals as the dependent variable, with gender and homeownership as the key independent variables, to explore the relationship between these factors. The model results are presented in <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="T0006" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Table 6</button>.
</p><div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 6. </span> Binary logistic models of migrant workers’ subjective perceptions.</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="T0006-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="/action/downloadTable?id=T0006&doi=10.1080%2F10225706.2025.2606824&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="T0006" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table">Display Table</a></div></div><p></p><p>In Models 3 and 4, the core variables were introduced into the models without considering other control variables. The regression results indicate that, compared to male migrant workers, female migrant workers find it easier to marry locals. Furthermore, the results of Model 4 show that migrant workers with homeownership in the local area also find it easier to seek a local spouse. Next, in Model 5, this study incorporates both core variables along with other control variables into the model. The regression results show that the signs of the coefficients for the core variables, gender and homeownership, remain unchanged compared to the previous models. Such results are consistent with the findings from the literature review and aligns with our expectations.</p><p class="last">The role of homeownership in the marriage market differs significantly between men and women. In China’s traditional culture, it is typically the man's responsibility to provide the marital home, which is seen as a critical indicator of his financial capability and readiness for marriage (Wei and Zhang <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0072" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>). Owning a home enhances a man’s status in the marriage market, as it signals his ability to offer security and stability for his future family. For women, homeownership is generally not expected; instead, they often consider a partner’s ability to provide a home as an important factor in choosing a spouse (Mu and Yeung <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0058" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>). This expectation aligns with traditional gender roles where men are seen as the primary providers, while women are viewed as seeking economic security through marriage. Building on Model 4, Model 5 introduces the interaction term “gender x homeownership” to explore the differing importance of homeownership for male and female migrant workers in finding a local spouse. The regression results show that the coefficient of the interaction term is positive but not statistically significant. This indicates that while both male and female migrant workers who own a home at their destination perceive it as easier to marry a local, the effect of homeownership does not significantly differ between genders. As illustrated in <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0002" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig">Figure 2</button>, without homeownership, women are more likely than men to feel that finding a local spouse is easier. When homeownership is factored in, this situation does not change, and both men and women experience a clear increase in perceived ease. The increase is consistent for both genders, with no statistically significant difference, which suggests that homeownership is equally important for female migrant workers as it is for male migrant workers. This result is inconsistent with our expectations and will be further discussed in the following section.
</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 2. </span></span> Predictive margins of homeownership#gender.</p></div><a href="#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="F0002"><img id="d1e1702" src="/cms/asset/8bcdb886-29ba-4e8e-bc95-e5bf2c8c9f37/rage_a_2606824_f0002_oc.jpg" loading="lazy" height="270" width="500" alt="Figure 2. Predictive margins of homeownership#gender."></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="F0002" data-popup-event-type="fig">Display full size</button></div></div><p></p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S005"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e1705">Discussion</h2><p>In today's youth marriage market, the logic of the market economy has fundamentally transformed the traditional matchmaking model based on reputation and trust within close-knit communities. As Becker (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0007" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1981</a></span>) explains in his theory of the economics of marriage, individuals make rational decisions in the marriage market, seeking partners who can maximize their economic and social utility. What was once a system built on social connections has now shifted to one in which assets, particularly property, play a central role. Bourdieu’s (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0010" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2011</a></span>) theory of social capital further supports this shift, suggesting that, in modern economies, social capital tied to familial networks and reputation is increasingly replaced by material assets as the basis for forming relationships. Love, as the foundation of marriage, has been increasingly externalized into tangible conditions that potential partners must meet. Due to the status-symbol nature of homeownership, a woman's property in China becomes a form of capital that enhances her attractiveness in the marriage market. Owning property grants a woman bargaining power, giving her greater autonomy and agency in selecting a partner, as Oppenheimer (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0060" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1988</a></span>) argues in her studies on how economic independence shifts traditional gender dynamics in relationships. Moreover, the fact that owning property garners more attention in the marriage market is significant, as in today’s high housing cost environment, property not only symbolizes social status and economic power but also represents future financial security and the possibility of achieving a higher quality of life. Women who own property clearly gain more decision-making power and agency in choosing a partner, with homeownership playing an empowering role in this process.</p><p class="last">Moreover, property ownership functions as a significant bargaining tool for women within the context of marriage. The quest for equality in familial and marital relationships has been a central focus of family studies for decades (see Harris <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0043" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2003</a></span>; Rosenbluth, Steil, and Whitcomb <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0063" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>; Wilcox and Nock <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0073" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2006</a></span>). For unmarried women who purchase property or married women who contribute financially to the purchase of a marital home, these actions are often motivated by the desire to secure a more equitable position within the household. The resource theory provides a useful framework for interpreting these dynamics, positing that marriage is fundamentally an exchange relationship, in which each partner contributes resources to satisfy mutual needs (Aida and Falbo <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0001" href="#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference"><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1991</a></span>). In this context, the partner with greater resources typically holds more power within the relationship.
